title: Survey Results
text:
The survey was conducted in the population of Aarhus, Denmark, and includes questions about beliefs, belief certainties, and preferences on five national topics: security, economics, welfare, immigration, and climate change. On Aarhus local topics, it has the ten most relevant questions from the Voting Advice Application (Kandidattest) for the municipal election.
Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggstats)
library(ggExtra)
library(scales)
library(gt)
library(patchwork)
library(glue)
data <- read_csv("survey_responses_ENG_TRANS.csv")

title: Survey Results
text:

Code

title: Survey Results
text:
1.2 Belief, Uncertainty, and Preference Distributions
Insights:

For all topics, beliefs are more skewed towards agreement than preferences.
Certainty about the beliefs is generally high.
Preferences have the typical pentamodal distribution spanning all possible opinions with peaks at the two extremes in the middle and two off-central moderate opinions (see Gestefeld et al. 2022). This maybe caused by some condensing around focal or socially emergent values.
Taking standard deviation (SD) as a measure of polarization, beliefs preferences are most polarized with Climate Change most and Immigration preferences least polarized. Beliefs are generally less polarized (partly a consequence of the positive bias) with Economic belief being most and Security belief being least polarized. On uncertainty there is the least variation in Mean and SD over all five topics.



Code
data_nat_long <- data |>
  pivot_longer(
    c(ends_with("_B"), ends_with("_P"), ends_with("_BCRT")),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Response"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Label = word(Variable, 1, sep = "_"),
    Type = word(Variable, 2, sep = "_") |>
      str_replace("BCRT", "Certainty") |>
      str_replace("B", "Belief") |>
      str_replace("P", "Preference")
  ) |>
  select(-Variable) |>
  left_join(nat_domains_questions, by = "Label")
data_nat_long_fractions <- data_nat_long |>
  count(Response, Label, Topic, Type, Preference_q, Belief_q) |>
  mutate(Fraction = n / sum(n), .by = c(Topic, Type))
data_nat_long_fractions |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Response, y = Fraction, fill = Fraction)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  facet_grid(Topic ~ Type)

title: Survey Results
text:
1.3 Belief-Preference Relation
Insights:

On economics and welfare the belief-preference relation is strongly positively correlated. (Who believes economic inequality is too high strongly tends to agree that the tax for the highest incomes must be raised; and who believes people who need public support do not always receive enough help tends to agree that the transfer income for the poorest cash assistance recipients must be increased.)
On security and climate change the belief-preference relation is moderately negatively correlated. (Who believes Denmark faces serious security threats is tends to disagree that Denmark spends too much money on supporting Ukraine; and who believes climate change poses an urgent threat to Denmark tends to disagree that nuclear power must be part of the energy supply.)
On immigration the belief-preference relation is essentially uncorrelated. (The belief that immigrants are not integrating well does not predict the preference for opening up more foreign labor non-European countries.)



Code
data_nat_belpref_fraction <- data_nat_long |>
  filter_out(Type == "Certainty") |>
  select(userId, Type, Topic, Response) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Type, values_from = Response) |>
  count(Belief, Preference, Topic) |>
  mutate(Fraction = n / sum(n), .by = Topic)

data_nat_belpref_fraction |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Belief, y = Preference)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Fraction, color = Fraction)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(weight = Fraction), formula = 'y ~ x') +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7) +
  scale_color_gradient(high = "darkgreen", low = "lightgray") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, by = 2)) +
  facet_wrap(~Topic) +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme(legend.position = c(1, 0), legend.justification = c(1, 0))








Figure 3: Belief-preference relation for the five national topics. Questions in Table 1.

title: Survey Results
text:
1.4 Belief Extremity and Certainty
Belief extremity is calculated as the absolute distance of the belief response from the neutral point (5).


Code
data_nat_extr <- data_nat_long |>
  filter_out(Type == "Preference") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Type, values_from = Response) |>
  mutate(Belief_Extremity = abs(5 - Belief), .by = Topic)
data_nat_extr_fraction <- data_nat_extr |>
  count(Belief_Extremity, Certainty, Topic) |>
  mutate(Fraction = n / sum(n), .by = Topic)


Insights:

Belief extremity and certainty are positively related for all topics in a very similar way. The overall correlation is 0.56.



Code
data_nat_extr_fraction |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Certainty, y = Belief_Extremity)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = Fraction, color = Fraction)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(weight = Fraction), method = "lm", formula = 'y ~ x') +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7) +
  scale_color_gradient(high = "darkgreen", low = "lightgray") +

title: Survey Results
section: 2.3 Principal Component Analysis on local preferences
text:
2.3 Principal Component Analysis on local preferences
Insights:

The Principal Component Analysis (PCA) shows PC1 capturing more than 30% of the variance of the 10 local preference items, and PC2 captures 12%, and PC3 and PC4 still slightly more than the average 10%.
PC1 has ALCL1 and ALCL9 strongly on the negative side and ALCL2-4 and ALCL6-7 on the positive side. (Note the sign of the PC loadings has no intrinsic positive of negative meaning). ALCL5 and ALCL8 are also on the negative side and ALCL10 loads very low on PC1. So, respondents with negative values in PC1 are in favour of raising taxes for welfare and on limiting car traffic, they also favour (mildly) mixing in schools and stopping the expansion of Aarhus Harbor, while they believe money can’t be saved in the public sector, these tasks should not given to private companies, running business need not be cheaper, construction of mosques need not be prevented, and no more parking space is needed. So, negative values of PC1 stand for a classical economically left and culturally liberal profile, and positive values for an culturally conservative/economically liberal profile. The question on the stadium is the only mostly unrelated topic on PC1.



Code
prcomp_pref_loc <- data |>
  select(paste0("ALCL", 1:10)) |>
  prcomp(scale. = TRUE)
prcomp_pref_loc$x <- prcomp_pref_loc$x |>
  as_tibble() |>
  bind_cols(data |> select(-...1))

prcomp_plot(
  prcomp_pref_loc,
  VOTE_LOC_PRTY,
  "Vote for Local Party",
  plot_heights = c(1, 2)
)

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text: The following steps are how data is used in the process of building and validating an agent-based model following Lorenz (2021). Figure 1 gives an overview of the process.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text:
1 Initialization
Setting up the foundational state of the model. The simulation environment is created and the initial values of its parameters are set. The agents are created and the initial states for their static and/or dynamic variables are set. Doing it data-driven means in the first place that the variables are analog to variables which are observable in the real world. This enables validation and calibration with empirical data. Data-driven initialization can also mean more specifically that the initial values of the variables are set based on empirical data. While this can be a starting point for a realistic simulation run, it goes againt the goal of having the model be able to reproduce the distribution of the variables as an emergent property of the model.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text:
2 Exploratory Data Analysis
Exploration of empirical data to understand the distribution of the variables and their relationships, and to identify stylized facts that the model should be able to reproduce. Done by visualizing, calculating standard summary statistics, and defining relevant targeted metrics.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text:
3 Validation
Data-driven validation is measuring a model’s ability to reproduce empirical stylized facts. This is also called assessing the replicative validity. Methods and metric can be similar as for macro-calibration (see below) but with a different focus. While calibration is model-internal parameter-tuning process to make it match data better, validation is a model-external assessment about its quality.

title: Data-driven agent-based modeling
text:
4 Calibration
Adjusting free parameters and simulation procedures such the the model matches its real-world subject better. Data-driven micro-calibration means that parameters and simulation procedures have realisitic microlevel foundations. Data-driven phenomenological macro-calibration means that parameters and simulation procedures are adjusted to match the stylized facts as quantifies be macrolevel metrics. While the former is imporant for counter-factual scenario studies, the latter is important for building forecasting models. Ideally, both do not lead to strong deviations but are consistent with each other.

title: Model Outline
text:
We build a stack of models that simulate the process of preference formation and an election in the electorate of the population of Aarhus. Once for the municipal election and once for the national election.
First, we will focus on the municipal election.

title: Model Outline
text:
5.1 Voting System
Besides the five emprical data sources, the Voting System is another source of empirical input. We implement the original Danish proportional voting system with open list composed by parties where each voter has one vote to either give to one candidate from a party list or just to one party list without specifying a candidate. Later the voting system shall be exchanged with other for counterfactual scenario simulations. The voting system has implications. The voting system determines the election setup (Model 4) based on the lists of candidates and, therefore, has implications on how the ballot looks and what voters have to decide about when they want to fill it out (Model 5). Subsequently it determines how the election results are computed from the ballots (Model 6).

title: Model Outline
text:
5.2 Initialization procedures
We have two initialization procedures. Both create a set of agents serving as a synthetic population representing the electorate of the city of Aarhus. Therefore, they both take the census data as input, such that they can create agents in the same magnitude and with demographic characteristics such that represent the real population. The procedures also take the survey data as input. This data is used to initialize agents also with relevant beliefs and preferences as the core dynamic agent variables and also with static internal variables of agents determining their behavior (to be explained later).
Initialization 1 is for initialization of the Agents for Preference Formation. The preference formation model will transform these preferences through individual preference updates. The goal is that the Agents for Voting have preference distributions and relations simular to the real world as captured in the survey data. The core dynamic variables model are therefore the preferences. That means the variables ALCL1, …, ALCL10. When the distributions and relations of these variables shall emerge through preference formation, the initial values of these variables should not be set based on the survey data but rather be initialized randomly around neutrality.
This implies the following guidelines for Initialization 1:

The variables ALCL1, …, ALCL10 shall be initialized as random numbers1 centered around neutrality (value equal to zero). The standard deviation of the distribution is a tuning parameter \(\sigma_\text{Pref}\). Roughly three settings are of interest:

\(\sigma_\text{Pref} = 0\) (default): All agents start with zero on all preferences and the distribution emerges through external input through news and candidates and through reinforcement.
\(\sigma_\text{Pref}\) close to zero: The initial values can serve as a small nudge.
\(\sigma_\text{Pref}\) as in the survey data: The preference formation model must than not produce variance but sort preference relations and specific distribution patterns beyond normal distributions.

The agents need some heterogeneity in relevant static internal variables determining their behavior. Candidates for such static variables are:

Three topics of interest as encoded in variable survey variable ALCL11. It could be encoded in ten binary variables marking if the topic is important for the agent.
A correlation matrix representing the mental model of the agent about the relations between the different preferences. This can be initialized based on the correlation matrix derived from different demographic and subgroups of repondents of the survey data. The mental model can then determine how like an update of preferences is when they perceive news, or the preferences of candidates and peers.
Long-term party preferences (taken, as a proxy, from the voting behavior as reported in the survey)

Variables derived from the survey data Part 3: Opinion on Politics specifying things like independence of political opinion formation or trust in others, curiousity for new opinions, propensity to proximity voting, preferences for people or parties, and other aspects. These aspects can be used to specify behavioral rules for agents in the preference formation model.


First version: ALCL1, …, ALCL10 are initialized as zero and a mental model for them as a correlation matrix taken from data and demographics. A few different correlation matrices are enough for the first version.
Initialization 2 is for initialization of the Agents for Voting. The voting model will transform these preferences and produces Agents with ballots. The goal is that the votes of the agents are similar to the real votes as captured in the survey data. The intialization procedure thus follows the main idea of a synthetic population with the same charaterstics as the real population. The simplest version would be by resampling from repsondents of the survey data. More sophisticated versions should be able to increase the diversity of agents in a realistic way.
Note: The Aarhus survey fulfills different roles in the Preference Formation and the Voting model. In the first, it is used mostly for validation of the outcome of preference formation and only a few aspects are used for agent initialization. In the second, the survey data is mainly used for intitialization while the empirical validation in the end is on the election results. That is the reason for Agents for Voting and Agents for Voting appearing two times in the simulation pipeline. This reflects that the pipeline is divided into the independent models of preference formation and the voting. At later stage, they can be combined into a single model.

title: Model Outline
text:
5.3 Validation functions
We have three validation functions. The first one is for validating the outcome of the preference formation model. The second one is for validating the votes of agents in the voting model, and the third one is for validating the election results.
Validation 1 The goal is that the distribution of simulated preferences and their relations are similar to the survey data. Therefore, we can use distributional similarity metrics and correlation similarity metrics as validation functions.
Validation 2 is for validating the votes of agents in the voting model. The goal is that individual voting decisions based on the preferences are similar to the actual voting decisions as reported by respondents in the survey. Therefore, we can use classification metrics as validation functions.
Validation 3 is for validating the election results. The goal is that the aggregated simulated election results are similar to the real election results. Therefore, we can use distance metrics between distributions as validation functions. The difference to Validation 2 is that we are not validating the individual votes but the aggregated election results.

title: Model Outline
text:
5.4 Simulation procedures
The Preference Formation model is a dynamic multi-timestep model where agents update their preferences based on their interaction but also with external input from news and candidates. Details are described
The Voting model is a one-shot model that takes the preferences of agents and the candidate and party profiles as input and produces a ballot (or an abstention) for each agent. In the default voting system the ballot is essentially a choice of one candidate or one party. In alternative voting systems, the ballot can be more complex.
The Election is the simple aggregation of all ballots to the typical voting outcome: Counts of votes for all parties and candidates and the vote shares of parties.

title: Model Outline
text:
6.1 Specification of the initialization
In the most basic version, the initialization of agents must include:

Dynamic variables: The preferences ALCL1, …, ALCL10 initialized as zero.
Static internal variables: A mental model for the preferences as a correlation matrix taken from data and demographics.

The preference variables in the survey all have values in \(\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}\), where -2 and 2 represent the strongest negative and positive preferences, respectively. In the simulation model, we use continuous values in the same range \([-2, 2]\). The latter allows for more fine-grained updates.

title: Model Outline
section: 6.2 Specification of the preference formation model functions
text:
6.2 Specification of the preference formation model functions
The simulation loops over several time steps. In each time step, agents broadcast their preferences and perceive the news and the preferences of their peers. Based on this input, they update their preferences.
A broadcasted news item has the same format as a broadcasted preference of an agent: It is a key-value pair where the key is one of the ten preference topics ALCL1, …, ALCL10 and the value is a number in the range \([-2, 2]\) like ALCL1: 1.5.
Each timestep is separated into two phases. In the broadcasting phase, the broadcast function writes out the preference in an internal variable broadcasted such that it can be read by agents in the perception phase.
In the simplest version (where we do not have a news dataset), broadcast(news) selects a random key and a random value.
The simple version of broadcast(preference) is that the agent picks a random key and takes its current the writes out its current preferences.
In the perception and update phase, the perceive function reads the broadcasted news and preferences of peers. The updatePreferences function then updates the preferences based on the perceived news and peer preferences.
In the simple version, perceive(news) and perceive(peers) both are followed directly by an update function updatePreferences for the own preferences. In the simple version, perceive(peers) selects a random other agent to perceive its broadcasted preference.
Given a perceived preference and the own preference profile updatePreferences updates the own preference of the same key or not by the procedure as specified by Batzke et al. (2025). Central for this is a mental model specifying the correlation between different preferences which the agent considers relevant. (To be derive from data next.)
